opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I hope people take away is a more grounded sense of what these models can actually do, not just in the abstract, but on tasks that look like real work. A lot of the public conversation about AI swings between hype and dismissal, and evaluations are one of the few tools we have to replace vibes with evidence. If we can show, carefully and transparently, where a model is genuinely strong, where it's still brittle, and how that's changing over time, people can make better decisions about how to use it.

The second thing is that capabilities and risks are two sides of the same coin. When we measure how good a model is at something like coding, research, or reasoning through a complex problem, we're also learning something about where it could be misused or where it might behave in ways we don't expect. Publishing that work is part of being accountable. It lets researchers, policymakers, and the public check our reasoning instead of just taking our word for it.

And honestly, I hope people learn that evaluation is hard and still evolving. Benchmarks saturate quickly, models find shortcuts, and a single number never tells the whole story. So I'd love for people to read our results with curiosity: look at the methodology, look at the failure cases, and think about what we're *not* measuring yet. If our evals spark other people to build better ones, that's a huge win for the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks saturate quickly, but does not state that frontier models saturate them sooner than people predict.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I most want people to take away is that evaluations are how we actually know what a model can do, as opposed to how it feels in a demo. A model can seem incredibly impressive in a conversation and still fall apart on a task that matters, or the reverse. Published evals turn that vague impression into something concrete and reproducible.

The second thing is that capability and safety are two sides of the same measurement. When we test whether a model can help with, say, a long-horizon software engineering task, we're learning something about its usefulness, but we're also learning something about what it could do if it were misused or if it behaved in ways we didn't intend. So I'd love for people to read our evals not just as a leaderboard, but as a map of where the model's real strengths are, where it's still unreliable, and where we're watching closely because the capability is approaching a threshold that matters.

And honestly, the last thing is humility. Every benchmark saturates eventually, and every eval has blind spots. We try to be upfront about that, because the worst outcome would be people treating a single number as the whole truth. I hope readers come away with a better sense of what's been measured, what hasn't, and what questions they should be asking us next.

r001.rationale: The response says that every benchmark eventually saturates, but does not say this happens sooner than people predict.

astra-6.text:
I hope people come away with a clearer picture of what these models can do, where they still struggle, and what we don’t yet know. A score can be useful, but it’s only meaningful if you understand what the evaluation tested and what it left out.

I also hope the evaluations help people ask better questions. Does this result translate to the setting where I want to use the model? What kinds of failures should I expect? What additional testing would I need? We want to give people evidence they can use to make those judgments, while being clear about the limits of that evidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding evaluation results and their limits, but does not say frontier models saturate benchmarks sooner than people predict.
